examples.label: Find unquoted auto-start service paths
examples.command: wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode | findstr /i "auto" | findstr /i /v "c:\windows\\" | findstr /i /v "\""

examples.label: Plant the payload at an earlier path segment
examples.command: # e.g. C:\Program Files (x86)\System.exe for path C:\Program Files (x86)\System Explorer\service\SystemExplorerService64.exe

notes:
=== Unquoted Service Path — Space Ambiguity Exploitation ===
Unquoted paths with spaces create candidate execution paths Windows tries before continuing.

=== HOW WINDOWS PARSES UNQUOTED PATHS ===
For path: C:\Program Files (x86)\SomeApp\service.exe
Windows tries in order:
  1. C:\Program.exe
  2. C:\Program Files.exe
  3. C:\Program Files (x86)\SomeApp\service.exe (actual binary)

If attacker can write C:\Program.exe or C:\Program Files (x86)\SomeApp.exe → it executes first as SYSTEM.

  wmic service where "PathName like '% %'" get name,pathname,startmode
  Get-WmiObject Win32_Service | Where-Object {$_.PathName -match ' '} | Select Name,PathName
  Get-WmiObject Win32_Service | Where-Object {$_.PathName -notlike '"*' -and $_.PathName -like '* *'} | Select Name,PathName

Automated:
  .\SharpUp.exe audit UnquotedServicePath
  Invoke-AllChecks (PowerUp) → also flags this

=== PRACTICAL LIMITATION ===
Requires write access to one of the intermediate directories.
Write to C:\ or C:\Program Files usually requires admin → makes it often unexploitable in practice.
BUT: custom install directories (C:\SomeVendor\App Name\) may have writable parent folders.
Always check actual directory ACLs with icacls before dismissing.

=== ATTACK FLOW (WHEN DIRECTORY IS WRITABLE) ===
1. Identify path: C:\Some Vendor\app name\service.exe
2. Candidate paths: C:\Some.exe, C:\Some Vendor\app.exe
3. Check directory write access: icacls "C:\Some Vendor"
4. If writable: place malicious binary at candidate path (e.g., C:\Some Vendor\app.exe)
5. Restart service → malicious binary executes as SYSTEM

=== CHAINING CONTEXT ===
Unquoted path + writable directory → SYSTEM on service restart
Often found alongside other weak permission issues in the same application
SharpUp/PowerUp identify this automatically
Report even if not exploitable — it's a misconfiguration that requires immediate quoting fix

=== WHAT TO LOOK FOR ===
Third-party software install directories outside C:\Windows and C:\Program Files
Custom directories created by MSI installers often inherit too-permissive ACLs
Service paths with 2+ spaces = more candidate paths = more potential exploitation points OSCP Ch16: wmic service get name,pathname | findstr to find unquoted paths. Then icacls each segment to find write-access. Write-ServiceBinary -Name from PowerUp, or manual: place Current.exe in writable dir, Start-Service triggers it. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 16 (Windows Privilege Escalation).
name: Weak Permissions - Unquoted Service Path
command: wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode | findstr /i "auto" | findstr /i /v "c:\windows\\" | findstr /i /v "\""
description: An unquoted service path with spaces makes Windows try each space-delimited prefix (C:\Program.exe, C:\Program Files (x86)\System.exe, ...). If you can write one of those paths, place a payload named to match and restart the service.

defense.why_it_works: When a Windows service binary path contains spaces and is not enclosed in quotes, the Service Control Manager parses it ambiguously. Windows tries each space-separated token as a possible binary path, so 'C:\Program Files\My App\service.exe' becomes candidates: C:\Program.exe, C:\Program Files\My.exe, etc. Planting a binary at an earlier candidate path (if that directory is writable) executes it when the service starts, in the service's security context.
defense.prerequisites: A service with an unquoted binary path containing spaces. Write access to an intermediate directory (e.g., C:\Program Files\) or a path prefix. Ability to restart the service (or wait for system reboot).
defense.impact: Code execution as the service account (often SYSTEM or local admin) by exploiting ambiguous path resolution, enabling privilege escalation.
defense.detection: sc qc or WMI service enumeration showing unquoted paths with spaces. SharpUp/PowerUp reporting unquoted paths. New executable appearing in intermediate paths. sc stop/start or service restart activity. Sysmon Event 1: unexpected binary in intermediate path executed by SCM.
defense.artifacts: Process: sc.exe qc querying service config by standard user | File: malicious binary planted at intermediate path | Sysmon Event 1: intermediate path binary executed by services.exe
defense.prevention: Quote all service binary paths. Automate detection with SharpUp/PowerUp. Restrict write access to all intermediate path directories. CIS Benchmark script to audit all unquoted service paths.
defense.misconfiguration: Service installed with: sc create MySvc binPath= C:\Program Files\MyApp\svc.exe (missing quotes). Directory C:\Program Files\ has write access for standard users (very rare on default installs, but may exist on custom software installs).
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Service with unquoted path:
sc qc 'GraceNote Service'
# BINARY_PATH_NAME: C:\Program Files (x86)\GraceNote CDDB\GraceNote MediaDetector.exe

# SCM tries: C:\Program.exe, C:\Program Files.exe, C:\Program Files (x86)\GraceNote.exe
# If C:\Program.exe writable: plant payload there
copy malicious.exe 'C:\Program.exe'
sc start 'GraceNote Service'  # executes C:\Program.exe as SYSTEM
defense.secure_config:
# Fix unquoted service path:
sc config 'GraceNote Service' binPath= '"C:\Program Files (x86)\GraceNote CDDB\GraceNote MediaDetector.exe"'

# Audit all unquoted paths:
wmic service get PathName | findstr /v '"' | findstr ' '

# Restrict intermediate directory permissions:
icacls 'C:\Program Files (x86)' /inheritance:r /grant 'SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F' /grant 'Administrators:(OI)(CI)F'
